documents.title: Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies fourth consensus report

chunks.content: Introduction Parkinson disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, affecting over 10 million people globally. With aging populations, its prevalence is expected to double by 2040, increasing burdens on healthcare systems and caregivers. Although PD is primarily defined by motor symptoms such as bradykinesia, rigidity, and tremor, non-motor features—particularly cognitive impairment—contribute significantly to morbidity – . Cognitive decline affects up to 80% of patients, with many progressing from mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI) to Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD) within a few years of diagnosis – Cognitive deficits in PD have serious clinical and societal impacts, including reduced quality of life, loss of independence, and higher rates of institutionalization. Healthcare costs for patients with PDD are twice those without dementia, and caregivers face increased psychological and financial strain. Predicting cognitive decline remains challenging due to heterogeneous disease progression. Early identification of at-risk patients is crucial for timely intervention, counseling, and improving clinical trial design , – . Current prognostic tools poorly predict cognitive outcomes in PD. Clinical scales like the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) focus on motor symptoms and offer limited insight into cognitive decline. While Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers and neuroimaging provide some prognostic value, they are invasive, costly, and impractical for routine use , . In contrast, blood-based biomarkers are minimally invasive, cost-effective, and feasible for repeated assessments , . Neurofilament light chain (NfL), a marker of axonal injury, correlates strongly with CSF levels and is linked to disease severity and cognitive decline in PD – . Similarly, total tau (t-tau) and phosphorylated tau181 (p-tau181) have been associated with cognitive dysfunction – . Prior studies have reported elevated plasma NfL and t-tau in individuals with PD who exhibit early cognitive deficits, and combinations of plasma α-synuclein, p-tau181, and Aβ-40 have been proposed as potential biomarkers – . However, the vast majority of these investigations rely on cross-sectional data, limiting their predictive power. Longitudinal biomarker trajectories, such as changes in NfL and t-tau, may better reflect disease progression , , yet few studies have evaluated their predictive utility in early PD or combined them with clinical data to improve prognostic accuracy . Advances in machine learning (ML) have transformed neurodegeneration research by enabling the analysis of complex, high-dimensional data – . ML can detect non-linear patterns and interactions often missed by traditional methods . Prior work using data from the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) has shown that ML models can achieve high accuracy in predicting disease progression by incorporating multimodal data, including motor scores, biospecimens, and patient-reported outcomes . However, the utility of ML for predicting cognitive decline in early PD using time-varying blood biomarkers remains underexplored. Building on our prior work predicting cognitive decline in early PD using baseline features (AUC = 0.93) , we now specifically investigate whether longitudinal trajectories of plasma NfL and t-tau improve prognostic accuracy beyond static baseline measurements. To capture their trajectories in a parsimonious way despite limited repeated measures, we summarized them using minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation values. Using data from the Early Parkinson’s Disease Longitudinal Singapore (PALS) cohort, we apply multiple ML algorithms to model cognitive decline over five years. Our objectives are to: (1) evaluate the predictive utility of longitudinal biomarker dynamics, (2) identify key predictors using advanced feature selection, and (3) develop a clinically relevant risk prediction tool. Results Baseline Characteristics and Descriptive Statistics by Outcome A total of 193 participants with early PD were included. At baseline, the mean age was 63.8 years (SD = 8.9), 58% were male, and the median education duration was 11 years (IQR = 8–15). The mean MoCA score was 25.4 (SD = 2.8). Disease severity was mild to moderate: 62% in HY stage 1, 30% in stage 2, and 8% in stage 3. Over five years, 44 participants (22.8%) experienced cognitive decline (Table ). Higher education (≥10 years) was protective (OR = 0.4; 95% CI: 0.2–0.7; P = .006), while elevated blood pressure increased risk: lying DBP (OR = 2.6; 95% CI: 1.3–5.2; P = 0.009), standing DBP (OR = 2.1; 95% CI: 1.1–4.3; P = 0.045), and lying SBP (OR = 2.1; 95% CI: 1.1–4.3; P = 0.045) (Table ). Feature Selection Analysis To identify the most predictive variables, thirty candidate features were assessed using three feature selection methods. The RF approach identified twelve variables, including years of education, lying and standing DBP, and four summary statistics (minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation) for both NfL and t-tau, along with baseline p-tau181 levels (Fig. ). The ShapleyVIC method selected fourteen predictors, which included t-tau (minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation), NfL (minimum and mean), as well as baseline MoCA score, hyperlipidemia, coffee and alcohol consumption, lying and standing DBP, p-tau181, and gender (Fig. ). The RF approach identified twelve variables, including years of education, lying and standing DBP, and four summary statistics (minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation) for both NfL and t-tau, along with baseline p-tau181 levels (Fig. ). The ShapleyVIC method selected fourteen predictors, which included t-tau (minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation), NfL (minimum and mean), as well as baseline MoCA score, hyperlipidemia, coffee and alcohol consumption, lying and standing DBP, p-tau181, and gender (Fig. ). The XGBoost-based method identified eleven key features, including the full set of summary metrics for both NfL and t-tau, lying and standing DBP, and years of education (Fig. ). Notably, eight variables—minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation of t-tau; minimum and mean NfL; and lying and standing DBP—were consistently selected across all three methods. Model Performance and ROC Analysis ML performance varied across algorithms and feature sets, with the most important finding being that models using longitudinal biomarker summaries (Model 1) consistently outperformed those using only baseline variables (Model 2), with AUCs ranging from 0.640 to 0.763 vs 0.465 to 0.560, respectively—validating our central hypothesis that biomarker dynamics better capture disease progression than static measurements (Table ). Models 1 and 3–7 incorporated biomarker measurements collected at baseline, year 3, and year 5; these models are therefore intended to support risk stratification during follow-up rather than strict baseline-time prediction. For some participants whose cognitive decline began before later biomarker collections, those year-3 or year-5 values may reflect biomarker levels concurrent with or shortly after onset, which we acknowledge as a methodological limitation. The XGBoost model using RF-selected variables (Model 4) achieved the highest AUC (0.806; 95% CI, 0.663–0.949) and the best overall performance, with accuracy of 0.730, sensitivity of 0.875, specificity of 0.690, F1 score of 0.583, and a Brier score of 0.140. The LightGBM model using time-varying biomarker summaries (Model 1) performed well (AUC = 0.763; 95% CI, 0.598–0.928), as did both LightGBM and XGBoost models using SHAPvIC-selected variables (Model 5; AUC = 0.698 for both). These models showed comparable sensitivity and specificity to the top-performing XGBoost model, though with slightly lower precision and calibration. Notably, the reduced SHAPvIC subset (Model 6), comprising six variables, achieved the highest specificity (0.862; 95% CI, 0.683–0.961) with XGBoost, highlighting the utility of parsimonious models in clinical prediction. Calibration of the Predictive Models Figure shows calibration results for Model 4, based on top predictors selected via RF. XGBoost and LightGBM demonstrated the best calibration, with mean absolute errors < 0.05 and close alignment to the 45-degree reference line, indicating well-calibrated predictions. The RF model was reasonably calibrated but showed deviation in lower predicted probabilities. In contrast, KNN and NN models were poorly calibrated, underestimating risk in high-risk individuals and overestimating in low-risk cases. Summary of Key Findings In the best-performing model—XGBoost using RF-selected variables—key predictors included years of education, lying and standing DBP, four summary statistics (minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation) for both NfL and t-tau, and p-tau181 levels. SHAP visualizations showed that elevated and variable t-tau levels strongly influenced high-risk classification. Supine and upright DBP ≥ 90 mmHg also contributed substantially. While NfL features were associated with cognitive decline, they were less frequently among the top three predictors. Overall, incorporating longitudinal biomarker summaries—especially dynamic t-tau features—improved predictive performance and enabled more parsimonious models suitable for clinical application. Discussion In this prospective study of early PD, we predicted a longitudinal outcome—5-year cognitive decline—using primarily baseline clinical and biomarker predictors, with only limited repeated-measures biomarker data incorporated. The two blood biomarkers with repeated assessments (t-tau and NfL) were measured at three time points and summarized using descriptive statistics (minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation) to provide restricted longitudinal information suitable for ML. Thus, the term “longitudinal” in this study refers to the outcome definition and the inclusion of summarized repeated biomarker measurements, rather than comprehensive trajectory modelling of all predictors. Integrating these longitudinal blood biomarker summaries significantly enhanced cognitive decline prediction using ML, directly addressing current limitations in PD prognostic tools. The XGBoost model with RF-selected features achieved the best performance (AUC = 0.806), a substantial improvement over the baseline-only model (AUC = 0.560), validating our hypothesis that biomarker dynamics outperform static measurements. This model also demonstrated the highest F1 score (0.583) and the lowest Brier score (0.140), reflecting both balanced predictive power and strong calibration. While Model 5 achieved higher specificity, its complementarity with Model 4 suggests that ensemble strategies may be a valuable future direction, an approach we highlight as an extension beyond the present analysis. While the absolute AUC (0.806) is lower than that reported in our prior baseline-only study (AUC = 0.93), the current findings represent a more robust and clinically translatable advance. While Model 5 achieved higher specificity, its complementarity with Model 4 suggests that ensemble strategies may be a valuable future direction, an approach we highlight as an extension beyond the present analysis. While the absolute AUC (0.806) is lower than that reported in our prior baseline-only study (AUC = 0.93), the current findings represent a more robust and clinically translatable advance. By incorporating longitudinal biomarker dynamics rather than relying solely on static baseline features, we reduce the risk of overfitting and provide a framework better aligned with real-world prediction and trial enrichment strategies. While the integration of longitudinal biomarker summaries (e.g., t-tau and NfL dynamics) significantly improved predictive performance (e.g., Model 4: AUC = 0.806 vs. Model 2: AUC = 0.560), we acknowledge that the inclusion of year 3 and year 5 measurements in Models 1 and 3–7 may capture concurrent changes for participants who experienced cognitive decline before these time points. This could shift the interpretation of these models toward associations with cognitive status rather than purely predictive relationships. However, with only 22.8% of the cohort experiencing decline spread across the five-year follow-up, such temporal overlap is likely infrequent, as most participants remained cognitively stable through year 3 or beyond, suggesting that most biomarker measurements contribute to predictive rather than concurrent associations. Model 2, which relies solely on baseline variables collected prior to any follow-up, ensures true predictive validity by using only pre-decline measurements. The moderate performance of Model 2 (AUC = 0.560) demonstrates the feasibility of early risk prediction, while the superior performance of models incorporating longitudinal biomarkers highlights the added value of capturing disease dynamics, with the caveat of potential concurrent influences in a small subset of cases. Across algorithms, dynamic changes in t-tau and DBP emerged as the most consistent predictors, providing actionable clinical insights for both individual patient care and therapeutic development. The consistent identification of t-tau features highlights tau pathology’s role in PD-related cognitive decline. Notably, t-tau variability was a strong predictor, indicating temporal fluctuations may reflect meaningful biological processes like axonal damage or inflammation. By summarizing NfL and t-tau trajectories using mean, minimum, maximum, and standard deviation, we were able to capture complementary aspects of biomarker dynamics—overall burden, extremes, and variability—each of which may carry distinct clinical significance in tracking disease progression. While these measures are mathematically related, they provide different biological insights: mean values reflect overall exposure, extremes may indicate critical thresholds or acute changes, and variability captures the stability of biomarker levels over time. Although CSF biomarkers are informative, blood-based assays offer minimal invasiveness and increasing reliability with technologies like Simoa. Our results support using serial plasma t-tau as a prognostic tool in PD, enabling longitudinal monitoring of neurodegeneration. Patients with rising or fluctuating t-tau levels could be candidates for further assessment or early intervention. The inclusion of NfL as a predictive biomarker also corroborates prior evidence of its value , . NfL reflects axonal injury and has been associated with faster motor and cognitive progression in PD , – . However, its predictive strength in our study was somewhat less robust than that of t-tau, suggesting that while NfL may capture broader neurodegenerative processes, tau-specific mechanisms may be more intimately tied to cognitive trajectories. These distinctions could be important in future therapeutic trials, where stratifying patients by biomarker phenotype may help tailor interventions or identify treatment responders. These t-tau dynamics have immediate clinical utility, enabling identification of patients who may benefit from cognitive monitoring or early intervention strategies. Beyond molecular biomarkers, our study reinforces the prognostic importance of DBP—both in lying and standing positions—as a consistent clinical predictor of cognitive decline. The association of elevated DBP with two-fold increased risk has significant clinical implications – . Autonomic dysfunction is common in PD and can lead to labile blood pressure patterns, including supine hypertension and orthostatic hypotension. These fluctuations may impair cerebral autoregulation, reduce perfusion to vulnerable brain regions, and accelerate neurodegeneration. Current PD guidelines focus on motor symptoms, but our findings support routine blood pressure monitoring to identify vascular risk and guide early intervention. More broadly, while current prognostic approaches in PD rely heavily on motor-focused assessments like the MDS-UPDRS, our blood-based model (AUC = 0.806) substantially outperforms typical clinical prediction tools for cognitive outcomes. This performance approaches that of invasive CSF biomarkers while offering significantly greater clinical feasibility, directly addressing the gap identified in current PD prognostic capabilities. Importantly, blood pressure represents a modifiable risk factor. Interventions such as midodrine, fludrocortisone, or domperidone may be used to address hypotension, while antihypertensives including ACE inhibitors or calcium channel blockers could be considered for elevated supine DBP, ideally under

This performance approaches that of invasive CSF biomarkers while offering significantly greater clinical feasibility, directly addressing the gap identified in current PD prognostic capabilities. Importantly, blood pressure represents a modifiable risk factor. Interventions such as midodrine, fludrocortisone, or domperidone may be used to address hypotension, while antihypertensives including ACE inhibitors or calcium channel blockers could be considered for elevated supine DBP, ideally under close monitoring to avoid worsening orthostatic symptoms. In patients with high DBP and fluctuating tau profiles, a multidisciplinary approach involving neurology, cardiology, and internal medicine may be warranted. The modifiable nature of blood pressure offers immediate intervention opportunities that could simultaneously reduce cognitive decline risk and improve cardiovascular outcomes in PD patients. Incorporating vascular health into PD management may not only reduce cognitive risk but also improve cardiovascular outcomes in this aging population. Another key finding was the protective effect of education, supporting the cognitive reserve hypothesis. Participants with ≥10 years of formal education had a 58% lower odds of cognitive decline than those with less education. While not modifiable retrospectively, educational attainment may aid in risk stratification. Individuals with limited education could benefit from closer cognitive monitoring, targeted interventions, and referral to neuropsychology. This finding supports risk stratification approaches where patients with limited education receive enhanced cognitive monitoring and support services. They may also be prioritized for emerging strategies to preserve cognitive function, including lifestyle modification, cognitive training, and digital therapeutics. Our results also point to the potential value of deploying ML-based prediction tools in clinical workflows. By integrating time-varying biomarker data, clinical measures, and demographic factors, ML algorithms can generate individualized risk scores that support early identification and proactive care. For instance, a PD patient with high DBP and rising t-tau levels could be flagged for cognitive rehabilitation or clinical trial referral, while a low-risk individual might focus on motor symptom management. These tools could be embedded in electronic health records (EHRs), providing decision support to clinicians and improving consistency in care delivery. Furthermore, ML-derived insights could enhance patient-provider communication, allowing neurologists to frame prognosis in more concrete terms, support advance care planning, and tailor surveillance strategies. In clinical trial design, our predictive model addresses critical challenges in PD therapeutic development. Current cognitive outcome trials suffer from heterogeneous disease progression, requiring large sample sizes and extended follow-up. Our model’s identification of 22.8% of early PD patients as high-risk, with 87.5% sensitivity and 80.6% AUC, could reduce required sample sizes by 60-70% through enrichment strategies while maintaining statistical power. This is particularly valuable for emerging anti-tau and anti-synuclein therapies where early intervention and precise patient selection are crucial for detecting treatment effects. Our findings also align with broader evidence suggesting that mixed pathology is common in PD, particularly in those with cognitive impairment , . While PD is defined pathologically by Lewy bodies composed of α-synuclein, many patients with dementia show concurrent tau and amyloid pathology on autopsy or PET imaging , . The observed importance of tau dynamics in our study supports this concept and may prompt reconsideration of PD as a disease spectrum rather than a single pathology . This perspective opens the door to cross-disease therapeutic strategies and biomarker-guided personalization of care, particularly for those who meet overlapping criteria for PD, dementia with Lewy bodies, or AD , . From a mechanistic standpoint, the interplay between vascular dysregulation and tau-driven neurodegeneration is particularly noteworthy. Chronic cerebrovascular dysfunction can disrupt glymphatic clearance of toxic proteins, promote blood-brain barrier breakdown, and create a permissive environment for tau aggregation. Conversely, tau pathology may exacerbate vascular reactivity deficits through endothelial dysfunction or oxidative stress. This bidirectional model suggests that targeting both pathways may offer synergistic benefits. For example, interventions aimed at reducing vascular stiffness or enhancing neurovascular coupling might complement disease-modifying therapies targeting tau aggregation or phosphorylation. Despite its strengths, this study has limitations. While we used rigorous internal validation, external validation in independent cohorts is needed to confirm generalizability. The primarily Asian composition of the PALS cohort may limit applicability to other populations. Biomarkers were measured at only three time points; more frequent sampling could enhance trajectory analysis. To enhance clinical interpretability, all baseline continuous variables (e.g., t-tau, NfL, DBP) were dichotomized using established clinical thresholds (e.g., DBP ≥ 90 mmHg) or ROC-derived cutoffs. While this approach aligns with clinical practice in PD, where binary risk categories facilitate patient stratification and intervention decisions, we acknowledge that it may reduce sensitivity to subtle variations and limit detection of interactions between variables, potentially decreasing statistical power. To enhance clinical interpretability, all baseline continuous variables (e.g., t-tau, NfL, DBP) were dichotomized using established clinical thresholds (e.g., DBP ≥ 90 mmHg) or ROC-derived cutoffs. While this approach aligns with clinical practice in PD, where binary risk categories facilitate patient stratification and intervention decisions, we acknowledge that it may reduce sensitivity to subtle variations and limit detection of interactions between variables, potentially decreasing statistical power. In future studies, we plan to incorporate continuous measurements or flexible modeling approaches, such as splines or interaction terms, to better capture nuanced biomarker dynamics while maintaining clinical applicability. Although the prospective design strengthens causal inference, the inclusion of time-varying biomarker measurements (NfL and t-tau) from baseline, year 3, and year 5 in Models 1 and 3–7 may include data that temporally overlap with or follow cognitive decline for some of the 44 participants (22.8%) who experienced decline over the five-year follow-up. This could overestimate predictive performance by reflecting associations with cognitive status at the time of measurement in a small subset of cases. However, given that only 22.8% of the cohort experienced decline spread across the five-year follow-up, such temporal overlap is likely infrequent, as most participants remained cognitively stable through year 3 or beyond, and the majority of biomarker measurements likely reflect pre-decline states. Model 2, which uses only baseline variables collected prior to any follow-up, ensures true predictive validity by relying solely on pre-decline data, mitigating this concern. Future studies could enhance predictive rigor by restricting longitudinal biomarkers to measurements collected prior to decline or by increasing the frequency of biomarker assessments to better isolate predictive signals. Another limitation of this study is the use of the MoCA as the primary cognitive outcome measure, which, as a screening tool, is designed for detecting clinically significant cognitive impairment rather than subtle changes in cognition. While the MoCA is sensitive to executive, visuospatial, and memory deficits common in early PD and contributed to our predictive models (e.g., via ShapleyVIC feature selection), its short format may reduce sensitivity to fine-grained cognitive changes. To enhance the detection of subtle cognitive decline in future studies, we plan to incorporate more comprehensive neuropsychological batteries, such as tests targeting specific executive or attentional domains, and increase the frequency of MoCA assessments to better capture longitudinal trends. These additions could complement the robust predictive power of longitudinal biomarkers (e.g., t-tau, NfL) and clinical measures (e.g., DBP) identified in our machine learning models, further refining risk stratification in early PD. A limitation of this study is the reliance on clinical criteria (NINDS for PD and exclusion of alternative dementias via history, examination, MoCA, and neuropsychological testing) without routine use of AD-specific biomarkers such as CSF or plasma amyloid-β42/40 ratios or amyloid PET imaging. While this aligns with the non-invasive design of the early PD-focused PALS cohort , , and the low baseline dementia prevalence in early-stage patients, it may not fully exclude subclinical AD co-pathology in a subset of participants. However, the rigorous clinical evaluations by movement disorders specialists, supported by frequent follow-up assessments every 4 months, enhance confidence in the specificity of PD diagnoses, even in the absence of amyloid biomarkers. Future studies incorporating amyloid biomarkers could further validate the specificity of PD-related cognitive decline trajectories identified here. A second methodological limitation involves the potential temporal overlap between biomarker measurement and cognitive decline onset in some participants. For individuals whose decline began earlier, part of the biomarker signal may reflect concurrent rather than strictly predictive information, which could slightly inflate apparent prognostic performance. This underscores the role of Model 2, which excludes follow-up biomarker values and therefore provides the strict baseline comparator. A third limitation is that we did not model biomarker changes using delta or slope features, nor did we perform full trajectory analyses. Although NfL and t-tau were collected at three time points, our sample size and event rate limited the feasibility of constructing reliable change-based or slope-derived predictors within an ML framework. We therefore summarized the repeated biomarker values using descriptive statistics to mitigate the risk of overfitting. Future studies with larger samples and denser biomarker sampling schedules could evaluate longitudinal change metrics and more granular trajectory-based modelling approaches, which may provide additional mechanistic insight. Finally, although we focused on interpretable features and avoided overfitting, future studies should assess whether adding biomarkers of synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, or α-synuclein activity improves prediction. Future research should prioritize replication in multiethnic cohorts, integration of imaging biomarkers (e.g., tau PET, diffusion MRI), and development of practical risk calculators for clinical use. Cost-effectiveness studies will be essential to evaluate the feasibility of widespread biomarker monitoring. As high-sensitivity blood assays become more accessible, their implementation will be facilitated by advances in digital health, cloud analytics, and decentralized data sharing. Methods Study Design and Participants, and Variables This prospective observational study used data from the PALS cohort, which tracks clinical, cognitive, and biological changes in early PD. The study employed a longitudinally defined outcome, while most predictors were collected at baseline. NfL and total t-tau were measured at three time points and summarized to provide limited repeated-measures information suitable for ML analyses. Participants were enrolled from specialist clinics in Singapore (2014–2018) and required a diagnosis of idiopathic PD within 1 year of enrollment, with symptom onset within 2 years, confirmed by experienced movement disorders neurologists using the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) clinical diagnostic criteria , , , . These criteria emphasize levodopa responsiveness, asymmetric onset, and the absence of features suggestive of alternative parkinsonian syndromes (e.g., early falls, pyramidal signs, or rapid progression indicative of multiple system atrophy or progressive supranuclear palsy). To ensure specificity for PD-related cognitive changes and rule out alternative dementias such as AD or dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), participants with any form of dementia other than potential Parkinson’s disease dementia at baseline were excluded based on comprehensive clinical evaluation, including detailed history, neurological examination, and cognitive screening with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA; baseline score ≥22 to exclude overt dementia) , , . This process incorporated red flags for non-PD dementias, such as predominant memory impairment with visuospatial sparing (suggestive of AD) or fluctuating cognition with prominent visual hallucinations (suggestive of DLB), as per established differential diagnostic guidelines , . Although cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or plasma amyloid-β42/40 ratios were not measured in this early PD cohort—consistent with the PALS protocol focused on non-invasive assessments , —the clinical diagnosis was supported by baseline neuropsychological testing in the context of MCI classification (using Movement Disorder Society Task Force Level II criteria for those with suspected impairment) . Exclusion criteria also encompassed comorbidities likely to confound outcomes or hinder follow-up (e.g., malignancy, unstable cardiovascular disease). Throughout the study, participants underwent review by trained neurologists every 4 months; any participant for whom alternative dementias (besides PDD) were suspected—based on evolving clinical features or ancillary testing—was promptly removed to ensure cognitive decline outcomes reflected PD-related changes , , , . Of the 214 participants recruited, 193 completed baseline assessments and had at least three years of cognitive follow-up, comprising the final analytic cohort. The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki. Approval was obtained from the SingHealth Centralised Institutional Review Board (IRB reference number: CIRB 2019-2433) and the National University of Singapore Institutional Review Board (IRB reference number: NUS-IRB-2022-899). Informed consent was obtained from all participants, ensuring that they were fully informed about the nature, purpose, and potential risks of the study. Participants underwent detailed annual evaluations over five years, including clinical, cognitive, and laboratory assessments. Cognitive performance was measured using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Venous blood samples were collected at baseline, year 3, and year 5. Primary biomarkers—NfL and t-tau—were quantified using ultra-sensitive single-molecule array (Simoa) assays. For these biomarkers, four summary features (minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation) were computed across time points to capture both levels and variability. Additional baseline biomarkers included suppression of tumorigenicity 2 (ST2), apolipoprotein E (APOE) genotype, p-tau181, and alpha-synuclein gene promoter repeat length (REP1). The primary outcome was cognitive decline, defined using two alternative criteria designed to capture clinically meaningful decline while addressing measurement variability concerns. Cognitive decline was defined as either: (1) a ≥ 1-point annual rate of decrease in MoCA score (calculated by dividing the total change from baseline by the number of follow-up years), or (2) a ≥ 1-point drop sustained across two consecutive years during the five-year follow-up period. The annual rate criterion ensures that clinically meaningful declines are captured regardless of follow-up duration (e.g., a 3-point decline over 3 years represents a 1-point annual decline). outcome was cognitive decline, defined using two alternative criteria designed to capture clinically meaningful decline while addressing measurement variability concerns. Cognitive decline was defined as either: (1) a ≥ 1-point annual rate of decrease in MoCA score (calculated by dividing the total change from baseline by the number of follow-up years), or (2) a ≥ 1-point drop sustained across two consecutive years during the five-year follow-up period. The annual rate criterion ensures that clinically meaningful declines are captured regardless of follow-up duration (e.g., a 3-point decline over 3 years represents a 1-point annual decline). The sustained decline criterion addresses potential measurement variability by requiring that decline patterns persist across multiple assessment periods rather than reflecting single-timepoint fluctuations. These alternative thresholds were selected to reflect subtle but clinically meaningful cognitive changes while distinguishing true cognitive decline from measurement noise – . Baseline demographic characteristics included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), years of education, smoking history, alcohol use, and consumption of coffee and tea. Clinical features comprised Hoehn and Yahr stage (HY), MDS-UPDRS Part III score, systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP and DBP) measured in both lying and standing positions, and comorbidities including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Importantly, only the baseline MoCA score was included as a predictor to account for participants’ initial cognitive status, while the outcome definition was based on longitudinal changes in MoCA scores over the follow-up period. This approach avoids circularity by distinguishing between initial cognitive performance (predictor) and subsequent cognitive trajectory (outcome). Cognitive decline, the primary outcome, was classified retrospectively at the end of the five-year follow-up using all available annual MoCA assessments. For the annual rate criterion (≥1-point decrease per year), the rate was calculated over the entire follow-up period. For the sustained decline criterion (≥1-point drop across two consecutive years), the onset was defined as the first year of the qualifying pair. In our cohort, 44 participants (22.8%) experienced cognitive decline over the five years. For models incorporating time-varying biomarkers (Models 1, 3–7), summary statistics (minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation) for NfL and t-tau were computed using measurements from baseline, year 3, and year 5. As cognitive decline could occur at any point during the follow-up, some year 3 and/or year 5 biomarker measurements may temporally overlap with or follow the onset of decline for some participants, potentially capturing concurrent associations rather than purely predictive relationships. However, given that only 22.8% of the cohort experienced decline spread across the five-year follow-up, such temporal overlap is likely infrequent, as most participants remained cognitively stable through year 3 or beyond, suggesting that the majority of biomarker measurements reflect pre-decline states. All continuous variables were examined for clinical interpretability and, when appropriate, dichotomized using clinically relevant thresholds: age >65 years, BMI > 25 kg/m², years of education ≥10, MoCA <26, and clinical definitions of hypertension for systolic and diastolic blood pressures. For variables without established cutoffs, the Youden index was applied to derive optimal thresholds from ROC curves to maximize sensitivity and specificity: ST2 = 14,200, total motor score = 38.9, and p-tau181 = 27.1. Statistical Analysis Missing data were addressed using a random forest–based imputation method . All preprocessing steps—including imputation, feature engineering, and variable selection—were performed strictly within the training folds during cross-validation; no information from the test set or outcome data was used at any stage of model training, thereby preventing data leakage. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize all variables. Continuous variables were presented as mean (standard deviation) or median (interquartile range), and categorical variables as counts and percentages. Associations between individual predictors and cognitive decline were assessed using univariate logistic regression, reporting odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For NfL and t-tau measured at three time points, we derived descriptive summaries (minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation) to capture overall level and variability across time. Given the small number of repeated measurements and cohort size, these features offer a parsimonious representation that is compatible with ML modelling and reduce the risk of overfitting compared with more granular change modelling. Alternative features such as delta or slope can be informative; however, change scores may be susceptible to measurement error amplification and regression-to-the-mean with sparse sampling. Our choice of summary features reflects a balance between interpretability, data constraints, and modelling stability. To identify the most informative predictors, we applied three complementary variable selection methods. First, RF importance scores were used to rank variables by mean decrease in Gini impurity, retaining only those above the average score. Second, the Shapley Variable Importance Cloud (SHAPvIC) method quantified each variable’s contribution using SHAP values; variables with 95% prediction intervals entirely above zero were selected. Third, we applied gain-based feature importance from Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), keeping variables with scores above the mean. To identify the most informative predictors, we applied three complementary variable selection methods. First, RF importance scores were used to rank variables by mean decrease in Gini impurity, retaining only those above the average score. Second, the Shapley Variable Importance Cloud (SHAPvIC) method quantified each variable’s contribution using SHAP values; variables with 95% prediction intervals entirely above zero were selected. Third, we applied gain-based feature importance from Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), keeping variables with scores above the mean. This triangulated approach enhanced both statistical robustness and consistency across methods. For predictive modeling, we trained five supervised ML algorithms: RF, neural network (NN), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), XGBoost, and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM). Each algorithm was evaluated across seven different feature sets: time-varying biomarkers alone; baseline variables alone; a combination of both; and subsets derived from each of the three variable selection strategies (including a reduced version of SHAPvIC for parsimony). The dataset was randomly split (80:20) into training and test sets, stratified by cognitive decline status. Hyperparameters were optimized via five-fold cross-validation on the training set. For RF, we tuned the number of trees and number of predictors considered at each split. For XGBoost and LightGBM, we optimized learning rate (0.01–0.1), number of boosting rounds (50–500), maximum tree depth (3–7), and L1/L2 regularization terms (range: 0–1). NN models varied in hidden layer size (1–5) and applied weight decay (0–0.1), while the optimal number of neighbors (k = 1–10) was selected for KNN models. Model performance was assessed on the held-out test set using multiple metrics. Discrimination was evaluated via AUC with 95% CIs from 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Additional metrics included sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and Brier score. The F1 score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, balances false positives and negatives. The Brier score quantifies the accuracy of probabilistic predictions. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated at the optimal threshold via Youden’s index. Calibration was assessed using decile-based plots comparing observed and predicted event rates across 10 bins. All analyses were performed using R version 4.2.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Statistical significance was set at a two-sided P -Value < 0.05. Ethical approval The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Institutional Review Board of SingHealth (IRB reference number: CIRB 2019-2433) and National University of Singapore (IRB reference number: NUS-IRB-2022-899).
